conversation.content:
Good morning—thank you for coming in today. My name is Maya, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I specialize in caring for new mothers, and it’s a privilege to sit with you.

I’ll be guiding us through a short screening tool called the Edinburgh Postpartum Depression Scale, or EPDS for short. It’s a well-studied set of 10 questions that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally during the past week. It isn’t a test, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever is true for you. Everything we discuss stays between us unless you tell me something that makes me worry about your immediate safety; in that case we would talk together about the safest next steps.

We’ll move through one question at a time. Feel free to ask me to repeat or rephrase anything. When you’re ready, we can begin.

To start: Over the last seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

[Soft half-smile, eyes a little tired]  
I’ve laughed a couple of times—like when my husband made a silly face at the baby—but it feels kind of forced. Most of the time I can’t really “get there,” even when something is objectively funny.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[slow head-shake, voice quiet]  
Not really… I mean, I chuckled once when the baby grabbed my husband’s nose, but it felt kind of distant, like I was watching someone else laugh. Mostly nothing feels funny anymore.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[shrugs, eyes on the floor]  
A few things, I guess—like my morning coffee or when my mom brings lunch—but even those feel kind of flat. I used to get excited about little plans, and now it’s more like “maybe that’ll be nice,” but the spark isn’t really there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[eyes well up a little, voice shaky]  
Yeah... I keep thinking if I were more "on it" the baby wouldn't have gotten that diaper rash, or I'd have the laundry folded, or I'd feel happier for my husband. Most days I end up telling myself I'm failing at being a mom at least once or twice.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[nods quickly, hands twisting in lap]  
Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly imagine she’s stopped breathing, or I’ll hear a siren and picture a car crash. There’s no real reason—it just pops in and I can’t shut it off for a while.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[presses palm against chest]  
A few times this week—like last night when she was asleep in the bassinet and the room was dead quiet. My heart started racing, I got sweaty, and I had to check her three times before the tightness in my chest eased. It felt like something awful was about to happen, but there was nothing there.
Things have been getting on top of me

[exhales shakily, shoulders sagging]  
Yes... most of the time. Dishes pile up, the baby needs changing, I haven't showered, and it all feels like a wave I can't out-run. I usually push through, but I'm running on empty and counting the minutes until the next nap.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[quietly]  
Yeah… I lie there after the last night-feed, exhausted but my mind keeps circling—did I sterilize the bottles right, is she gaining enough weight, am I already messing her up. It takes me an hour or more to drift off, and then I wake up again with my heart pounding for no clear reason.
I have felt sad or miserable

[eyes drop to the floor, voice thin]  
Most days I feel like I’m walking around with a gray cloud. I’ll cuddle the baby and still feel this heavy sadness in my chest. It isn’t every single moment, but it’s there more often than not.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[swallows hard, dabs corner of eye with sleeve]  
Twice this week it boiled over—once when she wouldn’t latch and once when my mom left after dropping off groceries. I just sat on the couch with tears running down, feeling like I’d never get anything right.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[long pause, voice barely above whisper]  
It... it’s flashed through my mind a couple of times, like "what if I just weren’t here," but I’ve never planned anything and I don’t want to leave her—I just want the heaviness to stop.

You've shared that the past seven days have felt heavy-laughter comes rarely and feels distant, excitement has flattened into a faint "maybe," and a gray cloud of sadness lingers even while you cuddle your baby. Daily waves of worry about her safety, sudden panic when the room is quiet, and racing thoughts at bedtime leave you exhausted yet unable to sleep. Overwhelming guilt whispers that you're failing as a mom, and twice this week tears spilled over as you sat on the couch feeling you'll never get anything right. A fleeting wish that the heaviness would stop has crossed your mind, though you quickly reassure me you don't want to leave her.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports almost no ability to enjoy humor, aligning with 'Definitely not so much now</sym>, <sym>Patient acknowledges minimal enjoyment from a few activities but describes them as "flat" and lacking the previous "spark," aligning with "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent daily self-blame for multiple parenting and household issues, matching 'most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient reports daily intrusive worries without real triggers, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple sudden episodes of intense fear with physical symptoms (racing heart, sweating, chest tightness) and repetitive checking, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most of the time," unable to keep up with basic tasks, and running on empty—aligns with "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty falling and staying asleep due to persistent anxious thoughts, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent sadness present "more often than not" and compares it to a "gray cloud" that lingers throughout most days, aligning with "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes two distinct crying episodes tied to feeling overwhelmed and inadequate, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports fleeting thoughts of not being here, indicating occasional self-harm ideation without intent or plan.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 25 falls well above the EPDS threshold of ≥14 that flags probable major <med>depression</med>. Item 10 scored 2, indicating <sym>passive suicidal thoughts</sym> and mandating immediate risk assessment. The clinical picture aligns with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: five-plus depressive symptoms present most days (depressed mood, markedly diminished interest, excessive guilt, insomnia, psychomotor agitation, fatigue, diminished concentration inferred from overwhelm) plus clinically significant distress and functional impairment. Co-occurring panic symptoms and intrusive worries suggest a likely <med>anxiety disorder</med> comorbidity. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or perinatal psychiatrist for full evaluation and safety planning
2. Call the <med>24-hour Postpartum Support International helpline</med> (1-800-944-4773) or local crisis line if distress escalates
3. Ask a trusted adult to stay with you and the baby until professional help is in place; remove firearms, large quantities of medication, or other lethal means from the home
4. Begin gentle scheduling: aim for one 3-4 hour block of night sleep using pumped milk or partner help; nap when baby naps; eat small protein-rich meals every 3-4 hours
5. Try 5 minutes of slow breathing or grounding (5 things you see, 4 you feel, 3 you hear, 2 you smell, 1 you taste) when panic rises
6. Schedule follow-up with this office within 48 hours to review mood, sleep, and safety plan
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Patient: Postpartum mother, infant <12 wks  
Date: [today]

Presenting Concerns (patient report)
- Marked loss of pleasure/interest (minimal laughter, blunted enjoyment of previously pleasant activities)
- Persistent low mood, described as “gray cloud,” with daily tearfulness
- Excessive guilt/self-blame regarding infant care; endorses “failing as a mom”
- Daily, intrusive, unrealistic worries (infant safety, catastrophes) → meets subjective “worried for no good reason”
- Episodic panic sensations (rapid heart beat, sweating, dread) in absence of trigger
- Overwhelm and sense of “running on empty”; difficulty completing daily tasks
- Sleep-onset and maintenance problems linked to racing, anxious thoughts
- Passive, transient suicidal ideation (“what if I just weren’t here”) without plan or intent; protective of infant

Screening Observations
- Consistent pattern suggests moderate–severe depressive symptoms with comorbid anxiety
- Safety factor: presence of self-harm ideation (passive) → warrants immediate risk assessment and safety planning
- Functional impairment evident (self-care, household tasks, caretaking confidence)

Risk Factors Identified
✓ Postpartum period  
✓ Anhedonia and pervasive sadness  
✓ Guilt / cognitive distortions  
✓ Anxiety/panic symptoms  
✓ Sleep disruption secondary to mood  
✓ Passive suicidal ideation  

Next Steps (for referral team)
- Complete Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) scoring; repeat safety evaluation
- Consider expedited referral to perinatal mental health specialty
- Provide crisis/safety resources and 24-hr contact information
- Coordinate with OB/pediatric team for follow-up within 48 hrs

Screening clinician: [Name, Credentials]
